* The measure of consumption used is the sum of the value of all foodstuffs, edible oil, and the  clothing, all in units of 1975 rupees per adult equivalent per year. These regressions use years (where available) 1975-1984. The counts in the middle columns of each set are the number of households for which one cannot reject $ \zeta = 1$ or $\zeta = 0$ at a 95% level of confidence. The counts in the left-hand columns of each set are the number of households for which one can reject $\zeta = 1$ or $\zeta = 0$ and for which the associated i statistic lies in the left-hand tail of its distribution. Finally, the counts in the right-hand columns are the number of households for which one can reject $\zeta = 1$ or $\zeta = 0$ and for which the associated  t statistic lies in the right-hand tail of its distribution. The null hypothesis that $\zeta=1$ is only sensible when $X_i^j$ has the same units as the measure of consumption: this is the case only for lines 1-5, 10-14, and 19-23.
